records.title: Choose a safe growing spot with the best soil
records.summary: Pick a small area on safe ground where digging went deepest, water does not rush through, and overflow cannot harm anyone.
instructions: Use the spots you marked during the probing check: the deepest, softest patches are best for pits.
Avoid the edges of the rise, drop-offs, and the main channels where red streams run.
Avoid low spots where water stands for days, unless you will build raised beds there.
Stay close to where you will store water, so carrying it is short.
Look downhill: if overflow from your plot would run toward a home, path or neighbour's land, choose another spot.
everyday_amounts: start with an area of a few paces by a few paces
limitations: The best spot can still have a hard layer close below; it only reduces the problem.
safety_notes: Keep away from edges, overhangs and unstable ground.
Never plan works that send water toward homes, paths or neighbours.
records.purpose: Put limited effort and organic matter where it has the best chance, and keep people and homes safe from runoff.
alternatives_if_missing: If you have no tools, use a strong stick and a flat stone to probe and mark spots.
expected_observable_change: A marked plot with the best spots flagged
Clear idea of where water will go when it overflows

task.label: Choose and mark the growing spot

records.title: Planting pits (where the hard layer allows)
records.summary: Dig planting pits about a forearm wide and as close to a forearm deep as the ground allows, in the softer spots, and fill them with soil mixed with organic matter.
instructions: Dig pits before the rains, at the spots you marked as softest or deepest.
Aim for about a forearm wide and a forearm deep. Where you hit the hard layer sooner, stop: do not force it.
Pile the dug soil on the downhill side of each pit as a small lip to catch runoff.
Space pits about a long pace apart in staggered rows across the slope.
Fill each pit with a mix of the dug soil, compost or manure, and leaf litter or chopped dry grass.
Leave the top of the filling a little below ground level so the pit collects water.
If water stood in your drainage check, cut a small notch on the downhill side so heavy rain can overflow.
everyday_amounts: about a forearm wide
about a forearm deep where the ground allows
about a long pace between pits
one to two bucketfuls of compost or manure per pit, mixed with the dug soil
a few handfuls of leaf litter or chopped dry grass per pit
limitations: Where the hard layer is continuous, pits stay shallow and can fill with water; raised beds are better there.
Digging pits is heavy work; build a few for a trial first.
safety_notes: Do not force tools through rock or jump on them.
Do not dig near edges or under overhangs.
Fill or mark open pits so people and animals do not fall in.
records.purpose: Create pockets of deeper, richer soil that also catch runoff, so roots have room and water around each plant.
alternatives_if_missing: No compost: use leaf litter, chopped dry grass, shrub prunings and any crop residue, layered in the pit.
No hoe: use a pointed stick and a flat stone to loosen and scoop gravel.
No bucket: carry fill in a cloth, basket or old sack and count loads.
expected_observable_change: Water collects in the pits after rain instead of running away
Soil in the pit stays darker and moist for longer after rain than the bare ground around it
Seedlings in pits grow taller and greener than any sown on bare ground

records.title: Knee-high raised beds
records.summary: Build soil upward instead of downward: heap soil, gravel-free fill and organic matter into beds about knee-high, edged with stones.
instructions: Mark beds about one arm-span wide (so you can reach the middle from both sides) and as long as you can fill.
Edge the bed with a low wall of stones or lumps of laterite.
Scrape loose topsoil from paths and bare ground nearby (not from slopes that will then erode) into the bed.
Layer in organic matter as you build: compost or manure, leaf litter, dry grass, small prunings.
Finish about knee-high, slightly domed, and cover the top with mulch.
On a slope, run beds across the slope; on flat ground with pooling, leave paths between beds as drainage lanes.
everyday_amounts: about knee-high
about one arm-span wide
several bucketfuls of compost or manure per pace of bed length
a thick layer of mulch, about a hand's depth when fresh
limitations: Gathering enough soil and organic matter is the main limit; start with one bed.
Beds dry out faster in the dry season; mulch is essential.
safety_notes: Lift stones with bent knees; watch for snakes and scorpions under them.
Do not strip soil from slopes or edges to fill beds.
records.purpose: Give roots more depth above the hard layer and keep them out of water that pools on it.
alternatives_if_missing: No stones: edge beds with logs, thick bundles of thorny prunings or packed earth ridges.
No compost: build in layers of leaf litter, dry grass and soil, letting them settle through the first rains.
Not enough soil: make shorter beds, or one bed only, rather than thin beds.
expected_observable_change: Beds stay above standing water after heavy rain
Roots grow down into the bed rather than sideways
The bed settles a little after rain; top it up with more organic matter

task.label: Build and fill knee-high raised beds

records.title: Containers and soil sacks
records.summary: Where the ground is one continuous rock sheet, grow a few plants in filled sacks, old containers or stone rings set on the surface.
instructions: Use old sacks, broken containers, or a ring of stones about a forearm across.
Make a few holes or gaps at the bottom so water can drain; set on a few flat stones.
Fill with a mix of scraped soil and organic matter, as for raised beds.
Place them close to stored water and in a spot sheltered from strong wind.
Mulch the top and water sparingly in dry spells.
everyday_amounts: each container or sack about knee-high when filled
about half soil and half organic matter by bucketfuls
limitations: Containers dry out fast and hold only a few plants; this is a trial or stop-gap, not a field.
safety_notes: Never use containers that held fuel, poisons or chemicals.
records.purpose: Provide rooting depth when the ground gives none, for a small trial or a few high-value plants.
target_constraints: no rooting depth on a continuous hard layer
alternatives_if_missing: No sacks: build a ring of stones a forearm high and fill it.
No compost: layer leaf litter and dry grass with soil.
expected_observable_change: Plants in containers establish while bare rock nearby supports nothing

task.label: Prepare and fill containers or sacks

records.title: Stone lines across the slope
records.summary: Lay lines of stones along the contour, across the slope, a few paces apart, to slow runoff so water soaks in and soil settles behind them.
instructions: Find the slope direction from the pour-water or first-rain check.
Mark a line across the slope that stays at the same level: walk across, checking water would not run along it.
Dig a shallow groove along the mark and set larger stones on the downhill side, packing smaller stones and gravel behind them.
Make lines about ankle to shin high, with no gaps where water can cut through.
Space lines a few paces apart; closer on steeper parts.
Before rains, decide where overflow will go and make sure it ends somewhere safe.
After each heavy rain, walk the lines: replace moved stones and fix any spot where water broke through.
everyday_amounts: lines about ankle to shin high
a few paces between lines, closer where steeper
limitations: Lines that are not level make water run along them and cut through at the low end.
Stone lines alone do not feed the soil; combine with organic matter and pits.
On flat ground where water pools, lines can trap water: use drainage and raised beds instead.
safety_notes: Never direct runoff toward homes, paths, neighbours' land or crumbling edges.
Lift stones carefully; check for snakes and scorpions.
Do not build near the edge of the rise or on unstable ground.
records.purpose: Capture the short season's hard rain on the plot and stop soil washing away in red streams.
alternatives_if_missing: Few stones: use lines of thorny prunings, bundled dry grass or crop stalks, or plant a grass strip along the line.
Work in stages: protect the planting area first, extend later.
expected_observable_change: Fine soil and leaves build up on the uphill side of the lines
Less red water leaves the plot after storms
Ground just above the lines stays moist longer after rain

task.label: Lay stone lines across the slope and check the overflow path

records.title: Handle pooling: raised planting and a safe overflow path
records.summary: Where water pools on flat ground, raise the planting areas and lead extra water along shallow drains to a safe place, instead of trapping it.
instructions: During or after heavy rain, mark where water stands and which way it slowly moves.
Build raised beds or mounds in pooling areas, and keep pits out of the lowest spots.
Scrape shallow drains, a hand deep or less, from the pools toward a safe low point away from homes and paths.
Where water collects safely, a covered container or a lined hollow can store some of it.
Check after each heavy rain that water drains within a day or two and drains have not cut deeper.
everyday_amounts: drains a hand deep or less
beds or mounds about knee-high in pooling spots
limitations: Drains must not start new gullies; keep them shallow and gently sloped.
safety_notes: Never send water toward homes, paths, neighbours or edges.
Stay out of moving water during storms.
records.purpose: Stop roots and seeds drowning on top of the hard layer while still using the water.
alternatives_if_missing: No tools: use a stick to scratch shallow drains and move gravel by hand.
If there is nowhere safe for water to go, raise planting higher rather than draining.
expected_observable_change: Standing water clears within a day or two after rain
Seedlings on raised spots stay upright and green

task.label: Mark pooling spots and plan a safe overflow path

records.title: Mulch: keep the soil covered
records.summary: Gather dry grass, leaf litter, crop stalks and prunings and keep a layer over pits, beds and between plants.
instructions: Start gathering before the rains: cut dry grass tufts (leave the roots), collect fallen leaves and shrub prunings.
Store it dry under a tree or weighted with stones so wind does not take it.
After sowing, spread mulch around (not on top of) seedlings once they are up.
Keep a layer about a hand's depth when fresh; top it up as it breaks down.
Keep mulch a finger's width away from stems to avoid rot and hiding pests.
everyday_amounts: a layer about a hand's depth when fresh
an armful per pit, several armfuls per pace of bed
limitations: Termites will eat mulch; that is part of how it improves the soil, but top it up often.
Mulch can hide pests and harbour rodents near stored grain; keep it in the field.
safety_notes: Do not gather grass from where snakes shelter without a stick to check first.
Keep mulch stores away from cooking fires.
records.purpose: Shield bare soil from hard rain, reduce crusting and runoff, keep moisture in through dry spells, and feed soil life.
alternatives_if_missing: No dry grass: use crop stalks, thorny prunings chopped small, or a scatter of gravel as a last resort.
Little material: mulch the planting pits and beds first, not the paths.
expected_observable_change: Soil under mulch is cooler and moist when bare soil is dry
Less crust forms after rain
Termites and other soil life work under the mulch, breaking it down

records.title: Compost or manure for pits and beds
records.summary: Mix compost or well-rotted manure into every pit and bed before sowing, measured in bucketfuls.
instructions: Use only well-rotted compost or manure: dark, crumbly and without a strong smell.
Mix it through the pit or bed fill, not in a layer on top.
Put more into pits where seedlings will be thinned to the strongest few.
everyday_amounts: one to two bucketfuls per pit
several bucketfuls per pace of raised bed
limitations: Compost improves fertility but does not by itself correct strong acidity.
There is no fixed recipe; watch how plants respond and adjust.
safety_notes: Wash hands after handling manure; keep it away from drinking water.
Fresh manure can burn seedlings and carry disease; let it rot first.
records.purpose: Supply nutrients and organic matter the poor, leached soil lacks, and help it hold water.
alternatives_if_missing: Not enough for all pits: fill fewer pits fully rather than all pits thinly.
No compost or manure: see the organic-matter alternatives.
expected_observable_change: Darker, crumblier soil in pits and beds
Greener, more even seedlings than in unfed spots

task.label: Mix compost or manure into pits and beds

records.title: Start with a small marked trial plot
records.summary: Mark a few pits or one bed as a trial, keep notes, and expand only after it shows results.
instructions: Mark the trial with stones or sticks: a few pits and, if possible, one raised bed.
Sow two or three different crops so you learn which suits the ground best.
If local advice says only trees grow here, include both a field-crop trial and a tree planting.
Keep a simple journal: date sown, rains, when seedlings came up, how they look each week.
Expand next season to the methods and crops that did best.
everyday_amounts: a few pits or one bed
two or three crops side by side
limitations: One season's trial can be thrown off by an unusual year.
safety_notes: Keep enough seed in reserve to re-sow if the first sowing fails.
records.purpose: Test what works on this ground (and test local claims) without spending all your seed, water and labour at once.
alternatives_if_missing: Few seeds: sow a few seeds of each kind and keep the rest back for re-sowing.
expected_observable_change: You can compare crops and methods on the same ground
Clear evidence for or against local advice

task.label: Mark a small trial plot and start a journal

records.title: Half-moon catchments on gentle slopes
records.summary: On gently sloping ground, dig half-moon shaped basins with the open side facing uphill and the soil piled into a curved bank downhill.
instructions: Mark a half circle a couple of paces across, with the open side facing uphill.
Scrape out the inside as deep as the ground allows (often less than a hand deep on laterite) and pile the soil on the curved downhill edge.
Line the curved bank with stones so it does not wash away.
Mix compost or organic matter into the inside and plant in the lower part of the basin.
Stagger half-moons so overflow from one is caught by the next below.
everyday_amounts: a couple of paces across
a bucketful or two of compost or organic matter inside each
limitations: Not for flat ground where water pools, or for steep slopes.
Too much rain can waterlog the basin; give it an overflow notch.
safety_notes: Never point overflow toward homes, paths or neighbours.
records.purpose: Collect runoff from the ground above into a basin where crops or a tree are planted.
alternatives_if_missing: No stones: compact the bank well and plant tufted grass on it.
expected_observable_change: Water stands briefly in the basin after rain, then soaks in
Plants in half-moons stay green longer in dry spells

records.title: Organic matter when there is no compost
records.summary: Without compost or manure, use leaf litter, dry grass, shrub prunings and crop residues, layered into pits and beds and left to rot in place.
instructions: Collect fallen leaves under trees and shrubs, cut dry grass, and chop prunings small.
Layer them into pits and beds with soil, wetting each layer if any water can be spared.
Dig in kitchen scraps (not meat or bones) and ash-free hearth sweepings.
Start a sheet-compost patch: pile residues in a shallow pit, cover with soil, and let the rains work on it.
If any animals are kept nearby, collect their droppings and let them rot.
everyday_amounts: several armfuls of leaves or grass per pit
a layer about a hand's depth through a bed
limitations: Raw material feeds the soil more slowly than compost; expect slower early growth.
Fresh green material can tie up nutrients for a while; mix it with soil.
safety_notes: Wear something on your hands when gathering thorny prunings.
records.purpose: Still add organic matter to poor soil when no compost is available, and start making some for later.
alternatives_if_missing: Very little material: concentrate it in a few pits for the trial.
expected_observable_change: Layers settle and darken over the first weeks of rain
Soil life (worms, termites) appears in the fill

task.label: Gather leaf litter, grass and prunings for pit and bed fill

records.title: Store rainwater in household containers
records.summary: Set clean, covered containers to catch rain from a roof, sheet or tarp so seedlings can be helped through dry spells.
instructions: Before the rains, clean every container that can hold water and find lids or covers.
Rig a sheet, tarp or roof edge so rain runs into the containers; weight the edges with stones.
Let the first rain wash dust off the roof or sheet before collecting.
Keep containers covered and in shade to stop mosquitoes breeding and to slow evaporation.
Use stored water sparingly: a cupful at the base of each seedling, early morning or evening, only in dry spells.
everyday_amounts: a cupful per seedling in dry spells
count how many buckets you have stored
limitations: Stored water is limited; it is for rescuing seedlings, not regular irrigation.
safety_notes: Never use containers that held fuel, poisons or chemicals.
Keep drinking water separate and covered.
Cover containers so children and animals cannot fall in.
records.purpose: Bridge the dry gaps that often follow the first rains and the dry spell mid-season.
alternatives_if_missing: No containers: dig a small hollow, line it with plastic sheet or packed clay, and cover it.
No sheet: collect from the lowest point where runoff gathers, after it has settled.
expected_observable_change: Containers fill during storms
Seedlings survive dry gaps that kill unwatered ones

records.title: Grow legumes in rotation or between cereals
records.summary: Include a legume such as cowpea or horse gram each season, between or after millet rows.
instructions: Sow cowpea or horse gram in some pits or between millet rows.
Next season, sow millet where the legume grew.
Return legume stalks and leaves to the soil after harvest.
everyday_amounts: alternate rows or alternate pits of cereal and legume
limitations: Benefits build slowly over seasons; one crop will not transform poor soil.
safety_notes: Do not eat seed that has been treated with chemicals.
records.purpose: Legumes can add nitrogen through their roots and help reduce striga on cereals.
alternatives_if_missing: No legume seed: ask neighbours for a handful to start a trial.
expected_observable_change: Cereals after legumes look greener
Fewer striga plants over seasons

records.title: Start a compost heap for next season
records.summary: Begin a compost pile or pit now from residues, leaves and scraps so next season starts with compost.
instructions: Dig a shallow pit or pile on level ground near the plot.
Lay coarse stalks at the bottom, then layers of leaves, grass, scraps and a little soil.
Keep it damp in the rains and covered with grass in the dry season.
Turn it when you can; it is ready when dark and crumbly.
everyday_amounts: a pile about knee-high
limitations: Composting slows in the dry season without moisture.
safety_notes: Keep it away from wells and drinking water.
records.purpose: Build a supply of compost, which is the main fertility input on this soil.
alternatives_if_missing: Little material: start small and add over the season.
expected_observable_change: Material shrinks, darkens and turns crumbly over the season

records.title: Optional: a small handful of wood ash or crushed shell per pit
records.summary: If you have it, a small handful of wood ash or finely crushed shell mixed into each pit fill may ease acidity a little. It is optional and must be used sparingly.
instructions: Use only ash from plain wood fires (not from plastic, painted or treated wood, charcoal briquettes or rubbish).
Mix a small handful into the whole pit fill, a couple of weeks before sowing if you can, not in a pile.
Crushed shell (egg or snail) must be crushed as finely as possible; it acts slowly.
Do it once per season at most, and watch how plants respond.
Skip it entirely if you have none: compost and tolerant crops matter far more.
everyday_amounts: a small handful per pit, mixed through
at most once per season
limitations: This is not a measured liming treatment; nobody can say how much acidity it corrects without a test.
Too much ash can harm seedlings and lock up nutrients.
Ash left in the rain loses much of its effect.
safety_notes: Wood ash is caustic: keep it out of eyes and off skin; avoid windy days.
Do not put ash directly against seeds or seedling roots.
Never use ash from burned rubbish, plastic, or treated wood.
records.purpose: Give a cautious, small nudge against likely acidity using household materials.
alternatives_if_missing: None available: skip this step; rely on organic matter and acid-tolerant crops.
expected_observable_change: No reliable change can be seen directly; plant response over weeks is the only clue

task.label: Optional: mix a small handful of ash or crushed shell into each pit

records.title: Optional: repeat the baking-soda fizz test on filled pit soil
records.summary: After pits are filled and a few weeks of rain have passed, repeat the baking-soda fizz test on filled pit soil. A weaker fizz is a hopeful sign, not proof.
instructions: Take a small spoonful of wet soil from a filled pit, put it in a cup or lid, and sprinkle on a pinch to a small spoonful of baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), using the same small amounts as the first time.
Watch for about a minute and compare with what you saw before treatment.
A weaker fizz than before is a hopeful sign, not proof that the soil is better; no change proves nothing either way.
Note the result in the journal. Do not delay planting for it.
everyday_amounts: a small spoonful of wet soil
a pinch to a small spoonful of baking soda
watch for about a minute
limitations: Weak evidence only: not a pH reading; never a reason to plant or not plant.
safety_notes: Do not taste the soil or the mixture; keep baking soda and soil out of eyes and mouth.
records.purpose: Give curious users an optional before-and-after clue, without making it a requirement.
alternatives_if_missing: No baking soda: skip it; watch the plants instead.
expected_observable_change: Possibly a weaker fizz than before (a hopeful sign only, not proof)

task.label: Optional: repeat the baking-soda fizz test on filled pit soil

records.title: Avoid: digging deep or trying to till or break the hardpan
records.summary: Do not try to dig deep, plough, or break up the hard layer across the plot.
instructions: Work with the shallow soil: build pits in soft spots, raised beds or containers.
If a tool bounces, stop and move a little to the side rather than forcing it.
limitations: Breaking a laterite sheet by hand is rarely possible, and broken pieces can re-harden after drying.
safety_notes: Forcing tools through rock causes injuries and broken tools.
records.purpose: Prevent wasted effort, broken tools, injuries and loss of the thin topsoil.
expected_observable_change: Less wasted effort; topsoil stays in place

records.title: Avoid: deep pits on a continuous rock sheet
records.summary: Where the hard layer is continuous, do not keep digging pits deeper; they will hold water like a bowl and can drown roots.
instructions: Build upward instead: raised beds, stone rings or containers.
If you already dug shallow pits, give them an overflow notch and fill them higher than the ground.
safety_notes: Do not force tools through rock.
records.purpose: Prevent waterlogged pits on solid rock.
expected_observable_change: No bowls of standing water around seedlings

records.title: Avoid: bunds or stone lines that trap water on flat ground that pools
records.summary: Where water already pools, do not build closed bunds, solid stone lines or deep basins that hold even more water.
instructions: Raise planting spots and give water a shallow, safe way out instead.
If stone lines are used at all, leave gaps and an overflow path.
limitations: Gentle slopes that also have some pooling need careful, permeable lines with an overflow.
safety_notes: Never send water toward homes, paths or neighbours.
records.purpose: Prevent drowning seedlings and rotting roots on top of the hard layer.
expected_observable_change: Water clears from planting spots within a day or two

records.title: Avoid: sending runoff toward homes, paths, neighbours or edges
records.summary: Never build lines, drains or bunds that push water toward homes, paths, other people's land or crumbling edges.
instructions: Before building any water work, follow where the overflow will end up.
End drains on safe, stable ground and spread the water out rather than concentrating it.
safety_notes: Concentrated runoff can undercut edges and cause collapses.
Stay away from channels during storms.
records.purpose: Protect people, property and neighbours, and avoid starting new gullies.
expected_observable_change: No new gullies; no water damage downhill

records.title: Avoid: large amounts of ash
records.summary: Do not pile ash onto beds or pits or use it as a main fertiliser.
instructions: If you use ash at all, keep to a small handful per pit, mixed through, at most once per season.
everyday_amounts: never more than a small handful per pit
limitations: Without a soil test, more ash is a guess that can do harm.
safety_notes: Ash is caustic; protect eyes and skin.
records.purpose: Prevent seedling damage and nutrient lock-up from too much ash.
expected_observable_change: Seedlings are not scorched by ash

records.title: Avoid: assuming compost or ash fixes strong acidity
records.summary: Do not assume compost, ash or shells have corrected the soil's acidity; nobody can tell without a test.
instructions: Keep choosing crops that tolerate acidic, poor soil.
Judge progress by how plants grow, not by assuming the soil is fixed.
limitations: Organic matter helps plants cope with acidic soil but does not neutralise strong acidity on its own.
records.purpose: Keep expectations honest so crop choice still favours acid-tolerant crops.

records.title: Avoid: burning grass and crop residue
records.summary: Do not burn dry grass or crop residues to clear the plot; keep them as mulch and organic matter.
instructions: Cut and lay residues as mulch, or add them to compost.
Only diseased residue should be removed; see regeneration guidance.
safety_notes: Fires on dry grassland spread fast and endanger people and homes.
records.purpose: Keep scarce organic matter on the soil and avoid bare, crusted ground.
expected_observable_change: More mulch and soil cover on the plot

records.title: Avoid: fresh manure or ash right against seeds
records.summary: Do not place fresh manure or ash directly where seeds go; it can burn seedlings.
instructions: Mix rotted material through the fill some time before sowing.
safety_notes: Wash hands after handling manure.
records.purpose: Protect germinating seeds.
expected_observable_change: Even germination

records.title: Test that mulched fill holds moisture
records.summary: Before sowing, check that a mulched pit or bed stays damp a finger deep a couple of days after rain or a bucketful of water, compared with bare ground.
instructions: Pick one finished pit or bed and one bare spot next to it.
After a rain (or after pouring a bucketful on each), cover the pit or bed with mulch about a hand's depth; leave the bare spot uncovered.
A couple of days later, lift the mulch and push a finger into the soil; do the same on the bare spot.
PASS: soil under the mulch is still damp and cool a finger deep while the bare spot is dry.
FAIL: both are equally dry: thicken the mulch, mix in more organic matter, and test again.
everyday_amounts: a bucketful of water per test spot
mulch about a hand's depth
feel a finger deep
limitations: A hot, windy spell can dry even mulched soil; repeat the test if the first one fails in extreme weather.
safety_notes: Check under mulch with a stick first in case of scorpions or snakes.
records.purpose: Confirm with your own hands that the fill and mulch will carry seedlings through short dry gaps, before seed is committed.
alternatives_if_missing: No spare water: wait for the next rain and test then.
No mulch yet: use leaf litter or a few stones laid flat as a temporary cover.
expected_observable_change: Soil under mulch stays damp for days longer than bare ground

task.label: Test that mulched pit or bed soil stays damp

records.title: Make a layered compost heap
records.summary: Build a heap of alternating dry brown material and green scraps with a little soil between layers, keep it damp like a wrung-out cloth, and turn it now and then until it is dark and crumbly.
instructions: Pick a shaded, level spot near the plot, away from wells and drinking water.
Lay coarse stalks or twigs at the bottom so air can get in.
Add layers: a layer of dry leaves or grass, then green weeds, fresh leaves or kitchen scraps, then a handful or two of soil; repeat.
Add aged animal droppings if you have them.
Keep it as damp as a wrung-out cloth: sprinkle used wash water in dry weather, cover with grass in hard sun.
Turn it with a stick every week or two, moving the outside to the middle.
Ready signs: dark, crumbly, smells of earth, and you can no longer recognise the scraps. In warm weather this usually takes a couple of months.
everyday_amounts: a heap about knee-high
a handful or two of soil between layers
damp as a wrung-out cloth
limitations: Slows almost to a stop when dry; plan it for the wet weeks.
Only well-rotted compost goes against seeds and roots.
safety_notes: Keep meat, bones, fat and human waste out of the heap.
Keep it away from wells and drinking water.
records.purpose: Produce mature compost, the main fertility input for pits and beds on this soil.
alternatives_if_missing: No green scraps: use fresh weeds and shrub leaves.
No water to spare: build it at the start of the rains and let rain keep it damp.
expected_observable_change: The heap warms and shrinks in the first weeks
Material darkens and crumbles
It smells earthy, not sour

records.title: Pit or trench compost
records.summary: Compost in a shallow pit or trench: fill it with layers of leaves, residues and scraps, cover with soil, and let the rains rot it in place.
instructions: Dig a pit or trench about a forearm deep where the ground allows (stop at the hard layer).
Fill with layers of dry leaves, green material, scraps and a little soil; cover with soil and grass.
Leave it through a rainy season; it is ready when dark and crumbly.
Trench option: bury scraps in a shallow trench beside a bed and plant above it after a few weeks.
everyday_amounts: about a forearm deep where possible
limitations: Slower than a turned heap; usually ready only after a rainy season.
safety_notes: Mark or cover open pits so no one falls in.
records.purpose: Make compost with less watering and less work than a heap, and enrich the spot it is buried in.
alternatives_if_missing: Shallow ground: make a covered pile instead.
expected_observable_change: Darker, softer soil where the pit or trench was

records.title: Overflow notch in pit lips and bed walls
records.summary: Cut a small, stone-lined notch in the downhill side of each pit lip or bed wall so heavy rain spills out at one safe point instead of drowning roots or bursting the wall.
instructions: Find the lowest point of the pit lip or bed wall on the downhill side.
Cut a small notch there, about a finger-joint lower than the rest of the rim.
Line the notch and the ground just below it with flat stones so spilling water does not dig a hole.
Make sure the spill leads to a safe, stable place, never toward homes, paths, neighbours or edges.
After a heavy rain, check that water left through the notch and no wall broke.
everyday_amounts: a notch about a finger-joint lower than the rim
limitations: A notch cannot fix a pit dug into a basin that floods; move or raise that planting spot.
safety_notes: Never point overflow toward homes, paths, neighbours or edges.
records.purpose: Keep roots out of standing water over the sealed hard layer and stop walls washing out.
alternatives_if_missing: No stones: pack the notch with tough grass clumps or crop stalks.
expected_observable_change: Pits and beds empty of standing water by the next morning
Walls stay intact after storms

records.title: Pit chains on gentle slopes (build one section at a time)
records.summary: On a gentle, stable slope, set a few planting pits in a staggered chain so overflow from one is caught by the next, building and testing one short section before adding more.
instructions: Start with one short section of three or four pits in a staggered line across the slope.
Give each pit an overflow notch on its downhill side, offset so the spill reaches the next pit's catchment, not straight downhill.
Watch the section in a heavy rain: water should spread and soak, with no pit left full of standing water by morning.
Only if that works, extend the chain; never let the last pit spill toward homes, paths, neighbours or edges.
Do not chain pits on flat ground where water pools, or on steep slopes.
everyday_amounts: three or four pits per test section
pits about a long pace apart
limitations: A chain concentrates water toward its lower end; the last pit needs a safe spill.
safety_notes: Never build pit chains above homes or paths or near edges.
Stop and redesign if any pit stays flooded.
records.purpose: Spread runoff across several planting pits instead of letting it gather into a red stream.
alternatives_if_missing: No stones for notches: pack them with grass clumps.
expected_observable_change: Runoff spreads between pits instead of forming streams
Pits dry out within a day after rain
